subtype: Cannot see flaws in own project [Actor]
passage: The day before the science fair, Suraj Sir walked along the lab tables checking models. Naveen stood proudly beside his windmill, built over six evenings from ice-cream sticks and a toy motor. Sir tapped the blades. "They scrape the base, Naveen. If you raise the stand a little, it will spin freely." Naveen's ears went red. "It spins fine, Sir. I tested it at home." Sir switched it on. The blades turned twice, scraped and stopped. "See? It just needs a push," Naveen said, and pushed it. "Six days I worked on this." Sir left a small wooden block beside the model and moved to the next table. Naveen slid the block aside without looking at it.

qa.q: What did Suraj Sir leave beside the model?
qa.a: A small wooden block.

qa.q: Why did Naveen's ears go red when Sir pointed out the scraping blades?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and hurt, because after six evenings on the windmill the comment felt like criticism of him and all that effort, not just of the stand. 😳

qa.q: What choice could Naveen make with the wooden block before the fair?
qa.a: He could raise the stand for one test run. If the blades then spin freely, the windmill he worked so hard on only gets better.

qa.q: How might Suraj Sir feel when Naveen slides the block aside?
qa.a: He may feel a little disappointed, since he wants the model to work, but he chooses not to force it and leaves the fix within Naveen's reach.

grounding: A student resists a teacher's fix for a science model he spent days building, because the effort makes the flaw hard to see and the advice feel personal.

subtype: Cannot see flaws in own project [Actor]
passage: I'm Mohit, and I sit next to Divyansh in class six. For nine days he built a solar system out of thermocol balls and wire, painting every planet at home. On Monday, Ma'am held it up and said, "Lovely colours. But your Saturn is bigger than Jupiter, and the real one is smaller. Can you swap the sizes?" Divyansh said, "No, Ma'am, it looks better this way." She asked again, gently. He said the book was probably wrong. At lunch he didn't open his tiffin. He kept touching Saturn's ring. I don't know what he was thinking. I only know he didn't change it, and later he told me Ma'am "just doesn't like my work."

qa.q: How many days did Divyansh spend building the solar system?
qa.a: Nine days.

qa.q: What does Divyansh saying Ma'am "just doesn't like my work" suggest?
qa.a: He seems hurt, feeling the correction about Saturn is aimed at him and his nine days of effort, which makes the actual mistake hard for him to see.

qa.q: What small step could Ma'am take to help Divyansh accept the fix?
qa.a: She could first praise the painting and the days he put in, then ask him to check the planet sizes in the book himself, so the change feels like improving his work, not rejecting it.

qa.q: What is it like for Mohit to sit beside Divyansh that day?
qa.a: Mohit watches a friend skip lunch and keep touching Saturn's ring without knowing what is going on inside, and may be unsure whether to say anything.

grounding: A classmate watches a boy refuse a teacher's correction to a model he spent days on, taking the suggestion as dislike of his work.

subtype: Cannot see flaws in own project [Actor]
passage:
Sunday: Mahima spent the whole afternoon layering pebbles, sand and cotton inside a cut plastic bottle. She painted CLEAN WATER on the side and showed it to everyone at home twice.
Wednesday: Sharmila Miss poured muddy water through it in class. It came out brown. "Your sand layer is too thin, Mahima. Add more and it will work." Mahima folded her arms. "I've worked on it all week. It's perfect."
Friday: At the science fair, the filter dripped brown again in front of the judges. "The mud today is extra dirty," Mahima told them. She didn't look at the thin sand layer once.

qa.q: What did Mahima paint on the bottle?
qa.a: CLEAN WATER.

qa.q: Why might Mahima have blamed "extra dirty" mud at the fair?
qa.a: She felt defensive and embarrassed, because she had put so much work into the filter that admitting the thin sand layer was the problem felt like admitting her effort had failed.

qa.q: What went wrong on Wednesday, and what could Mahima have tried instead?
qa.a: She took the advice as an insult to her week of work and refused it. She could have added more sand as a quick test before Friday.

qa.q: What might Sharmila Miss be thinking as the filter drips brown on Friday?
qa.a: She may feel sorry that a simple fix was turned down and wonder how to help Mahima see the problem without feeling attacked.

grounding: Over a week, a girl refuses a teacher's fix to her water-filter model because her effort makes its flaw hard to accept.

subtype: Cannot see flaws in own project [Actor]
passage: Tenzin, you're sulking because Miss said your bridge model sags. Let your Nirmala Paati tell you about my periscope. I was eleven, in Coimbatore, and I spent four afternoons on it: cardboard, two mirrors from my mother's old compact, black paint inside. It was beautiful. At the science exhibition, our teacher looked through it and said, 'The top mirror is at the wrong angle, Nirmala. Tilt it and you'll see over the wall.' I said, 'It works fine!' She tried to show me. I took it from her hands. I felt she was saying I was stupid, not the mirror. I went home and cried. My brother tilted the mirror the next day while I was at school. It worked perfectly. I was angry for a week. So, kanna, is Miss talking about you, or about the bridge?

qa.q: What did the teacher say was wrong with Nirmala's periscope?
qa.a: She said the top mirror was at the wrong angle and needed tilting to see over the wall.

qa.q: Why did young Nirmala take the periscope from the teacher's hands?
qa.a: After four afternoons of work, she felt the teacher was saying she was stupid, not the mirror, so the suggestion felt like an insult.

qa.q: What could Tenzin try with Miss's comment about the sagging bridge?
qa.a: Tenzin could stop taking it personally, as Paati asks, and try Miss's suggestion to see if the bridge holds better.

qa.q: How might Nirmala's brother have seen the periscope?
qa.a: He probably saw only a mirror that needed tilting, without the hurt feelings, so fixing it seemed simple to him.

grounding: A grandmother tells how, at eleven, days of work on a periscope made her blind to its flaw and took a teacher's suggestion as a personal insult.

subtype: Cannot see flaws in own project [Actor]
passage: The school bus broke down on the flyover, and Gopika reached the science fair with only twenty minutes before judging. She set up her quiz board on the table, sweating: twelve questions, twelve bulbs, a week of evenings twisting wires. Sangeeta Ma'am came by and pressed question four. Nothing lit. 'One wire's loose at the back, Gopika. Tape it down and it'll work.' 'It works at home, Ma'am.' 'It isn't working now. Twenty minutes, quick.' Gopika felt her face go hot. 'You think I did it badly.' 'I think one wire is loose.' Gopika turned the board away. 'The judges will press other questions.' Ma'am left the roll of tape on the table. The first judge pressed question four. Gopika stared at the tape, wishing she had used it.

qa.q: How long did Gopika have before judging?
qa.a: Only twenty minutes before judging, because the school bus broke down on the flyover.

qa.q: Why did Gopika say 'You think I did it badly'?
qa.a: She felt hurt and embarrassed, hearing the comment about one wire as criticism of her week of evenings, which is why her face went hot.

qa.q: At which moment could Gopika have saved her project, and how?
qa.a: When Ma'am left the tape, Gopika could have taped the loose wire at the back in a minute before the judges came.

qa.q: How might Sangeeta Ma'am have felt when Gopika turned the board away?
qa.a: Ma'am may have felt frustrated and a bit sad, since she only wanted to help and could see the easy fix.

grounding: Under time pressure a girl refuses her teacher's simple fix for her science model because a week of work makes the fault hard to see and the advice feel personal.
